query: For a multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy exposed to simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperature, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain the accelerated coupled degradation and why it occurs? Specify a controlled comparison capable of distinguishing the proposed explanation, predict the changes in total degradation and the individual wear and corrosion responses relative to a matched baseline, define the relevant boundary conditions, identify supporting evidence, and give a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Under combined tribological contact and high-temperature corrosion, recurring fracture of protective oxide films at multi-phase interfaces—where galvanic coupling accelerates local dissolution—drives a self-sustaining cycle of oxidation, mechanical removal, and enhanced corrosion, which collectively results in rapid material loss from the eutectic high-entropy alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: A multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy with distinct phases (e.g., FCC + σ or other second-phase intermetallics) and a nominal protective oxide film at elevated temperature.
generation.intervention: Subject the alloy to simultaneous sliding wear and corrosive environment at an elevated temperature (e.g., ∼800 °C), ensuring repetitive mechanical disruption of oxide scales and exposure of fresh surfaces to corrosive media.
generation.conditions: Comparable contact loads, sliding speeds, and a salt-containing high-temperature environment to fully activate both wear and corrosion during the test.
generation.structural_mediator: Multi-phase interfaces that act as galvanic couples and sites for preferential oxide de-cohesion and local damage under combined mechanical and chemical stresses.
generation.mechanism: Mechanical removal of oxide films on the more anodic phases exposes fresh surfaces that dissolve preferentially due to local galvanic differences, promoting repeated formation and fracture of the oxide, thereby accelerating net material loss beyond the sum of independent wear and corrosion rates.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to a single-phase HEA or a test condition lacking corrosive species, the multi-phase eutectic alloy under simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperature will show a notably higher total degradation rate, with both wear loss and corrosion current elevated beyond simple addition of separate processes, revealing a strong synergy.
generation.baseline: A single-phase HEA of similar overall composition tested under identical mechanical and environmental conditions but without the interphase galvanic potential, or the same alloy exposed to wear-only or corrosion-only conditions.
generation.boundary: Synergistic wear-corrosion acceleration is most pronounced where the multi-phase microstructure exhibits significant galvanic mismatch and where oxide films are susceptible to mechanical disruption at moderately high temperatures (≈600–850 °C). Outside these phase contrasts or temperature ranges, oxide rupture and galvanic effects may diminish.
generation.uncertainty: Quantitative contributions of oxide disruption vs. galvanic dissolution vary with alloy composition and testing conditions; further systematic tests are needed to isolate each factor’s relative impact.

falsification_experiment.design: Compare a multi-phase eutectic HEA and a comparable single-phase HEA in a controlled tribocorrosion test rig at ∼800 °C with identical loads, sliding speeds, and corrosive medium. Monitor real-time friction, electrochemical potential/current, and post-test oxide morphology/chemistry.
measurements: Wear track volume loss and coefficient of friction (COF).
Open-circuit potential and potentiodynamic scanning data.
Microscopic and chemical analysis of oxide integrity and interphase boundaries.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the multi-phase alloy does not show a synergistically higher total degradation (i.e., no marked increase in combined wear-corrosion rate) compared to the single-phase reference, or if no localized oxide disruption and galvanic dissolution at interphase boundaries are observed, then the proposed mechanism is invalidated.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractThis work studies the fabrication of CoCrFeNiMo high-entropy alloy (HEA) coatings via coaxial powder-fed laser cladding, addressing porosity and impurity issues in conventional methods. The HEA coatings exhibited eutectic/hypereutectic microstructures under all laser power conditions. A systematic investigation of laser power effects (1750–2500 W) reveals that 2250 W optimizes microstructure and performance, yielding a dual-phase structure with FCC matrix and dispersed σ phases (Fe-Cr/Mo-rich). The coating achieves exceptional hardness (738.3 HV0.2, 3.8× substrate), ultralow wear rate (4.55 × 10−5 mm3/N·m), and minimized corrosion current (2.31 × 10−4 A/cm2) in 3.5 wt.% NaCl. The friction mechanism of the CoCrFeNiMo HEA coating is that in high-speed friction and wear, the oxide film is formed on the surface of the coating, and then the rupture of the oxide film leads to adhesive wear and abrasive wear. The corrosion mechanism is the galvanic corrosion caused by the potential difference between the FCC phase and the σ phase.Keywords: high-entropy alloy coatings, coaxial powder-feeding laser cladding, CoCrFeNiMo, laser power

In this study, bulk samples of a CrMoNbWV high-entropy alloy (HEA) were obtained for the first time by spark plasma sintering (SPS) of mechanically alloyed (MA) powders at 1200 °C, 1300 °C, and 1400 °C. Microstructure evolution, phase formation as well as wear and corrosion behavior were investigated. The MA powders’ phase composition was found to be represented by body-centered-cubic (BCC) solid solution. The solid solution partially decomposed to Laves phases under the sintering, such as Cr2Nb and (Fe, Cr)Nb, and NbVO4-VO oxides mixture. The temperature increase to 1400 °C led to a grain coarsening of the BCC phase and decreased the Laves phase content accompanied by precipitation at the grain boundaries. The sintered samples showed high hardness and compressive strength (2700–2800 MPa) at room temperature. The wear tests demonstrated excellent results in comparison to conventional wear-resistant composites. The obtained samples also exhibited high corrosion resistance under electrochemical tests in H2SO4 solution. In general, the temperature has an obvious influence on the corrosion behavior of the EHEA. Corrosion of the EHEA occurs in both regular and irregular patterns and exhibits apparent selectivity. Only the pitting appears at 5 ℃, while pitting and few selective dissolution regions are observed at 25 ℃. Furthermore, pitting and more selective dissolution zones occur at 40 ℃ and 60 ℃, indicating that an increase in temperature increases the rate of selective dissolution. decision.trend: Early work on eutectic high-entropy alloys introduced fine-scale microstructures combining multiple phases to balance strength and ductility (PMC4145285). Subsequent studies focused on high-temperature wear and oxidation behavior (PMC7515071), as well as combined wear/corrosion performance of multi-phase microstructures (PMC7866258). More recently, attention has turned to eutectic or near-eutectic coatings where galvanic effects and oxide formation have been tied to tribological and corrosion responses (PMC12156342). Overall, these efforts show that multi-phase EHEAs display excellent mechanical strength at elevated temperatures and can form beneficial oxide layers, but display accelerated material loss when wear and corrosion act concurrently, highlighting an unsolved synergy problem in multi-phase systems.
decision.unsolved: Despite evidence that micro-galvanic coupling at interphase boundaries and mechanically disrupted oxide scales both contribute to compounded material damage, no unifying single mechanism conclusively explains how wear-driven oxide removal accelerates corrosion, or how local chemistry/phase contrasts promote additional dissolution and mechanical removal.
decision.lever: Design a side-by-side tribocorrosion rig comparing multi-phase eutectic vs. single-phase reference HEAs under identical normal load, sliding speed, temperature (e.g., 800 °C), and corrosive environment (e.g., salt-containing atmosphere). Track in-situ friction, electrochemical current, and oxide film evolution.
decision.why: A well-controlled experiment isolating phase contrast (eutectic vs. single-phase), mechanical contact conditions, and corrosive environment will validate or refute the hypothesis that the interphase boundary galvanic potential and mechanical oxide debridement are jointly responsible for enhanced wear-corrosion synergy. If the eutectic alloy shows disproportionately higher total degradation and correlated local breakdown of the oxide alongside increased corrosion current (despite similar bulk composition), the mechanistic explanation is supported. If rates of wear and corrosion remain additive rather than synergistic, or if single-phase and multi-phase samples degrade similarly, then the hypothesis is falsified.
